questions.q: After a database restore, what happens to the DiskANN index on a SQL Server vector table?
options: It is restored byte-for-byte along with the table data
The index definition restores with the database, but the index contents rebuild from the vector column data during recovery
It must be dropped and recreated manually with different parameters
It is permanently lost and cannot be rebuilt
questions.explain: The DiskANN index definition is part of the database metadata and restores with the database, but the index contents rebuild from the vector data during recovery - at significant cost for large tables, making the rebuild a first-class RTO component.

questions.q: According to the chapter, how long can the DiskANN index rebuild take on a 50M-row table with 1536-dimensional indexes?
options: A few seconds, since it is a metadata-only operation
Several hours, depending on MAXDOP and memory
Roughly one minute per million rows, fixed
It never rebuilds; the secondary always takes over
questions.explain: On a 50M-row table with 1536-dimensional DiskANN indexes the rebuild can take several hours depending on MAXDOP and memory, so RTO must account for it separately from restore time - measured on a restore test, not estimated.

questions.q: How does a synchronous-commit Always On secondary benefit vector workloads compared to backup-and-restore?
options: It gives zero-data-loss failover with the DiskANN vector index warm and queryable immediately, since vectors and index changes replicate through the log stream
It skips log replication for VECTOR columns to save bandwidth
It stores embeddings in a cheaper object-storage tier
It eliminates the need for any backups
questions.explain: Vectors in VECTOR columns replicate through the log stream like any data, and the DiskANN index on the secondary stays in sync through redo - so a synchronous-commit secondary gives zero-data-loss failover with a warm, queryable index.

questions.q: What is the step teams most often skip in the chapter's cross-region failover runbook, and why does it matter?
options: Updating statistics after failover
Quiescing writers - pausing the embedding pipeline before failover, otherwise in-flight batches land on the old primary and are silently lost
Flipping the DNS CNAME
Running the recall canary
questions.explain: The most-skipped step is quiescing writers: failing over with the embedding pipeline still writing means in-flight batches land on the old primary after the flip and are silently lost to the new primary.

questions.q: In the DR runbook, how is the watermark for post-failover embedding pipeline catch-up determined?
options: From the SQL Server error log timestamp
SELECT MAX(EmbeddedAt) FROM dbo.DocumentChunks, recorded with the backup or at failover
From the differential backup file name
It is not needed; the pipeline restarts from the oldest document
questions.explain: The watermark is SELECT MAX(EmbeddedAt) FROM dbo.DocumentChunks - recorded with the backup and at failover - so pipeline catch-up knows where to resume re-embedding.
